transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I guess what brings me in is… I can’t seem to get past how rough and worn I look, especially my face and hands. The cracks and spots, the sagging—every time I’m around bank people or someone at the county office, I feel like they’re staring right at it. My wife tells me I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, which, you know, I have, for years… fields’ll do that to a person. But it doesn’t sit right with me. I can’t stop noticing it.
Do you feel that the way your face and hands look is abnormal or that something is wrong with them, even if others don’t seem to notice or are reassuring?

Yeah… I do. I mean, I know my wife says it’s just from working outdoors all these years, and maybe that’s true some, but when I look at my face or my hands, it looks wrong to me. Too cracked, too spotted, too saggy.

And then if I’m sitting across from a banker or somebody at the county office, I can’t hardly pay attention to what they’re saying because I’m thinking they’re looking right at it. Course, those offices always have that harsh lighting too—makes everybody look like they’ve been dug up out of the field—but still, I feel like mine stands out. I can’t seem to get past it.
Is your concern about your appearance limited to your face and hands, or do you feel similarly about other parts of your body?

Mostly it’s my face and hands, yeah. That’s what I can’t get past—the cracks and spots and how saggy everything looks, like I’ve been left out in the weather too long. I mean, I have been out in the weather, working fields and all that, and my wife says that’s all it is.

But when I’m sitting with a banker or somebody down at the county office, I just feel like they’re looking right at my face or my hands on the desk. Those places always have bad lighting too, you know, makes every little mark show up. But it’s those parts mostly that bother me.
Do these concerns about how your face and hands look ever lead you to avoid certain situations, or do they cause you a lot of anxiety that’s hard to manage?

Yeah… it does. More than I like to admit, I guess.

I’ve missed calls with bankers because I couldn’t get myself looking… acceptable enough to deal with them, even just over a call if I knew it might turn into sitting down in person. And I’ve put off farm decisions that needed making because I just couldn’t bring myself to go in and sit across from people with my hands out there on the desk.

And then there’s the retreat and the craft sales—my wife says photos help folks see what we’re doing, and she’s probably right, but I stopped agreeing to be in pictures. I just don’t want my face or hands shown like that. I know that sounds foolish, maybe, but it gets under my skin and I can’t shake it.
Have you ever felt similarly self-conscious or overly concerned about the way any other parts of your body look, outside of your face and hands?

Not really… I mean, I suppose everybody my age has things they don’t love looking at, but what brings me in is I can’t get past my face and hands.

It’s the roughness, the cracks, the spots, how worn and saggy they look. Like when I’m across from a banker or someone at the county office, I’m sure they’re staring at it, even though my wife tells me I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors his whole life. She says that like it’s supposed to settle it, and maybe it should, but it doesn’t.
How much time do you spend thinking about how your face and hands look, and does it feel like these thoughts are interfering with your daily life?

It’s… it’s a lot of the day, honestly. Not every single minute, I guess, because there’s chores and weather and machinery to think about—last week the pump was acting up and that took over for a while—but it keeps coming back.

What brings me in is I can’t get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. The cracks, the spots, the sagging… I’ll be trying to focus on something normal, like talking to a banker or someone at the county office, and I’m just sure they’re looking at my hands or my face instead of listening to me. My wife says I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, and maybe she’s right, but it still interferes. I spend too much time thinking about it, and it makes it hard to just go about my business.

Do these thoughts about your face and hands ever feel so intense or overwhelming that you have trouble functioning normally, like difficulty concentrating or completing tasks because you’re so focused on how you look?

Yeah… yes, I’d say it gets in the way. I don’t know if I’d call it “not functioning,” but I’ve definitely not done things I should’ve done.

I’ve missed calls with bankers because I couldn’t get myself feeling… presentable enough, I guess. And I’ve put off farm decisions because that meant sitting down across from people, with my face right there and my hands on the desk. Then I get thinking I should wash up again, or maybe wear different sleeves, or just wait until another day, and then another day goes by.

And with the retreat and the craft sales—my wife handles a lot of that, and she says pictures help, people like seeing who’s behind it. She’s right, probably. But I’ve stopped agreeing to be in photos, because I don’t want my face or hands shown. So, yes, it does make it hard to get things done sometimes.
Have you ever experienced periods of time where you felt persistently down, hopeless, or lost interest in things you used to enjoy, separate from how you feel about your face and hands?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I mean, I’ve had low spells, sure—at my age, with the farm and bills and the weather not doing what it’s supposed to, you get worn down. There was one spring where the rain just wouldn’t quit, and everybody in town was complaining, even the feed store guys were in a mood.

But separate from the face and hands… I don’t know. It’s hard to untangle, because when I feel bad, that’s usually where my mind goes. I don’t think I’ve noticed some whole separate stretch where I just lost interest in everything for no reason. At least not that I can say clearly.
Have your concerns about your face and hands ever caused problems in your relationships, work, or other important areas of your life?

Yes, it has. Mostly with work, I suppose, though it spills over at home because my wife ends up picking up the slack.

I’ve missed calls with bankers because I couldn’t get myself feeling like I looked acceptable enough to deal with them. Which sounds foolish when I say it out loud—farm business doesn’t wait just because a man doesn’t like his hands—but there it is. And I’ve put off decisions on the farm when it meant sitting down with people face-to-face.

And then with the retreat and craft sales, my wife’s always saying folks like to see who made something, or who runs the place. She’s probably right. But I’ve stopped agreeing to be in photos, because I don’t want my face or hands in them. So yes… it’s caused problems, more than I like to admit.
Do you feel that your concerns about your face and hands take up a lot of your time or feel very difficult to control, like you can’t stop thinking about them even when you try?

Yeah… it does take up a lot of room in my head. I’ll try to think about something else, and then I’m right back to my face or my hands.

It’s the roughness, mostly—the cracks and spots on my hands, and my face looking saggy or worn out. I know my wife says I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, which… I mean, I have. That’s not exactly shocking, working land and being in weather all these years. My father’s hands were the same way, actually—he could fix a gate with baling wire and make it hold longer than something new from town.

But when I’m around bankers or county people, I can’t get past the thought that they’re looking right at those things. Like they’re noticing every crack, every spot, every bit of wear. And once that gets going, it’s hard to shut off. I can tell myself to stop, but it doesn’t really listen.

Do you ever find yourself doing things like checking your face or hands repeatedly, trying to cover them up, or comparing them to other people’s hands or faces to try to feel better about how they look?

Yes… I do that. More than I probably ought to.

Before I leave for something like a loan meeting, or even when we’re setting up at a craft-fair table, I’ll check the bathroom mirror, then the truck mirror. I’ll turn my hat this way and that, trying to make my face look less… I don’t know, worn out, I guess. Like it makes any real difference.

And my hands—I catch myself looking at the younger workers’ hands, comparing mine to theirs. Which is silly, because they haven’t put in the years I have. But I’ll still do it, and then I’ve wasted time I should’ve been using on the farm. My wife will be waiting by the door, and I’m still fussing with a hat brim or looking at my hands like something’s going to change.
